source_read: PDF, pp. 710–714 (all pages; text extracted with pdftotext -layout; every number used checked on 150-dpi renders of pp. 710–713; Figure 1 read on a 300-dpi crop of p. 711; Tables 1–2 on the p. 712 render)

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of the findings: the claim keeps 'found' and 'named in the cause of death' apart from 'caused', as the source does. Three small wording points. (1) Among the reasons the authors give for calling the count a minimum, 'deaths in which it was not tested for or not alleged are not counted' is not stated by them: their reasons are 95% coroner coverage (p. 710), positive cases still awaiting inquiry or inquest, test sensitivity, and incomplete geographical coverage (p. 713). It is true by construction (only alleged deaths, and only those with mephedrone identified, are counted), so it should be worded as the editors' point, not attributed to the authors. (2) 'Other substances were found in 54 of the 62' is not printed: it is 62 minus the 8 with mephedrone alone (editors' calculation), and the magnitude's 12.9% and 58.1% are likewise editors' calculations (the paper prints 13% for 8 of 62 and no percentage for 36). (3) 'Specimens ... are not described' is slightly too strong: the Results do not name a specimen, but the Discussion calls the 38 quantified values post-mortem blood levels (p. 712); sampling site, interval after death, laboratories and methods are indeed not given.
claims.note: Every number in the statement and magnitude re-found and checked on the rendered pages: 128, 25, 13, 90, 69, 62; 8 alone; 36 in the cause of death, 18 on its own; alcohol 26, stimulants 22, hypnotics or sedatives 22, opioids 13, piperazines 13, other cathinones 13; Table 1 categories 26, 18 (11 hanging), 6, 5, 5, 2 (sum 62); verdicts 35, 11, 8, 5, 1, 1, 1 (sum 62); 95% coverage. Recomputed: 25/128 = 19.5%; 25/115 = 21.7%; 8/62 = 12.9%; 36/62 = 58.1%; 62 − 8 = 54. Points the claim could add or adjust: (a) in Scotland the Methods name the Scottish Crime and Drug Enforcement Agency as the data source since 2004 (and the General Register Office for Northern Ireland); procurators fiscal appear as the officials returning verdicts and in the acknowledgment, so 'from coroners and, in Scotland, procurators fiscal' is acceptable but the agency is the stated channel; (b) the presence route of the register's definition is for controlled drugs at post-mortem, and the paper places the UK classification of mephedrone in spring 2010 (p. 712), so for deaths before then mephedrone's presence alone did not meet that criterion; the paper does not say which criterion admitted each death, so 'could enter because mephedrone was present' is fair only as 'could'; (c) Figure 1 plots 123 suspected deaths against 128 in its caption and 35 deaths 'caused or contributed to by mephedrone' against 36 in the text (editors' sums of the printed monthly labels); (d) the authors' grouping counts 18 self-inflicted deaths while the coroners' verdicts include 11 suicides and 8 open verdicts; the paper does not reconcile the two; (e) the Discussion itself says mephedrone's precise causal role in the polydrug deaths remains unclear (p. 712), which supports the claim's caution.

anchors.extracted: Data from the National Programme on Substance Abuse Deaths (np-SAD) at St George's, University of London, which since 1997 receives coroners' information on drug-related deaths in the UK, Channel Islands and Isle of Man, and since 2004 also from the Scottish Crime and Drug Enforcement Agency and the General Register Office for Northern Ireland (about 25,000 deaths in all). 95% of coroners' areas in England and Wales report regularly (the abstract calls 95% an average annual response rate); the authors say the number of cases must be regarded as a minimum.

A death is recorded by np-SAD if at least one of: (a) one or more psychoactive substances directly implicated in the death; (b) a history of drug dependence or misuse; (c) controlled drugs present at post-mortem. Coronial inquest files include post-mortem and toxicology reports; internet searches of toxicology, newspaper and other media websites found further cases.

anchors.locator: Methods, continuation at top of left column
anchors.extracted: Media reports supplemented the np-SAD data collection form for several cases, especially where full coronial files could not be accessed; members of the London Toxicology Group were canvassed for cases; analysis covers concluded cases with forms submitted by 31 October 2011.

128 alleged mephedrone-associated deaths identified; mephedrone not found at post-mortem in 25; toxicology pending in 13; identified at post-mortem in 90, of which inquests concluded in 69 and forms received for 62, treated as 'confirmed fatalities' meeting the inclusion criteria. Editors' calculations: 25/128 = 19.5%; 25/115 with results = 21.7%.

Verdict or conclusion of coroners or procurators fiscal: accidental death or misadventure 35, abuse of drugs 5, suicide 11, open 8, homicide 1, natural causes 1, narrative 1 (sum 62). Deaths in England 46, Scotland 9, Northern Ireland 4, Wales 1, Guernsey 2.

Mephedrone formally included in the cause of death in 36 of the 62, on its own in 18; by post-mortem or ante-mortem results it was the only substance found in 8 (printed 13%; editors 12.9%). Other substances: alcohol 26, stimulants 22, sedatives or hypnotics 22, opiates or opioids 13, piperazines 13, other synthetic cathinones 13, antidepressants 8, antipsychotics 5 (Table 2 adds GBL/GHB 5, cannabis 5, ketamine 2, miscellaneous 9). Who wrote the cause of death and on what evidence is not stated. Editors' calculation: 36/62 = 58.1%.

Circumstances as grouped by the authors: acute drug toxicity after mephedrone alone or with other substances 26; self-inflicted harm 18 (means include throat cutting, gunshot, jumping from a bridge, intentional overdose; hanging in 11); bizarre or risky behaviour 6 (drowned trying to swim a river, driving under the influence, stabbed); collapsed at a party 5 (raised temperature recorded in 1); died in hospital days or weeks later 5 (3 from acute liver or multi-organ failure); risky sexual activity 2. Sum 62.

Mephedrone was identified at post-mortem in all 62 except one person who died in hospital 3 weeks after taking it; this conflicts with the Results' description of the 62 as drawn from the 90 with mephedrone identified at post-mortem.

Authors: a non-negligible share of alleged deaths turned out not related to mephedrone (they say because other drugs were identified); in the polydrug deaths mephedrone's precise role in causing death remains unclear.

Authors' limitations: positive cases still await inquiry or inquest; presence of mephedrone in post-mortem toxicology does not necessarily mean it caused or contributed to death; trends may reflect changes in coroners' methods or forensic technology; test sensitivity and specificity mean a negative result needs caution, so the count is likely an underestimate; incomplete coverage of coroners' jurisdictions; concentrations missing for some deaths (some may have had only traces); mortality rates per occasion of use not calculated, so the extent of risk cannot be determined.

anchors.locator: Results, 6th paragraph (p. 711, continuing p. 712); Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 712)
anchors.extracted: Concentrations quantified in 38; 37 summarised after excluding one value above 2000 mg/L (the text layer reads 92000; the page prints >2000): mean 1.938 mg/L (range <0.01–22.0); 10 'monomephedrone' cases mean 1.996 (<0.01–12.15); 27 combined cases mean 1.749 (0.03–22.0). The Discussion calls these post-mortem blood levels; no sampling site, interval after death, laboratory or method. Subgroup-weighted mean is 1.82, not 1.938 (editors' calculation).

Monthly series July 2009 to August 2011: printed labels of the suspected-death series sum to 123 (caption n = 128); confirmed-intake series sums to 62; series 'confirmed fatality caused or contributed to by mephedrone' sums to 35 (text: 36 with mephedrone in the cause of death). Editors' sums from a 300-dpi crop.

key_findings.correction: Wilson intervals recomputed: 13.6% to 27.2% and 15.2% to 30.1%, as stated.

Figure 1 sums re-read independently on a 300-dpi crop: confirmed-intake 62 (peaks 9 in March and 7 in July 2010), 'caused or contributed to' 35 (29 from September 2009 to June 2010, 6 from November 2010 to May 2011). Weekday arithmetic 11.5 against 5.3 per day confirmed.
Wilson intervals recomputed: 45.7% to 69.5% and 6.7% to 23.4%, as stated.

Small precision: the Results name no specimen, but the Discussion (p. 712, 4th paragraph) calls them post-mortem blood levels, so 'specimen not reported' is better 'specimen named only as blood, in the Discussion; sampling site, interval and method not reported'. The '>2000 mg/L' reading is confirmed on the render.

risk_of_bias.note: High for any statement about how many deaths mephedrone caused; the domain judgments (coverage 'no' for 28 of 90 positives unanalysed, 31%; measurement 'no') follow from the text.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial is defensible: 'confirmed' in the abstract and title reads as confirmation of a mephedrone death though it means presence, and the Discussion's psychosis/depression and 'other drugs identified' readings go beyond the results; the Limitations paragraph is candid.

missed: Criterion (c) of the register's definition is presence of a controlled drug at post-mortem; the paper places the UK classification of mephedrone in spring 2010 (p. 712, Discussion, 2nd paragraph), so for the deaths before then (about half of the 62 by Figure 1) mephedrone's presence alone did not meet that criterion; which criterion admitted each death is not reported (editors' inference from the paper's own dates; worth a line under selection effects).

The authors' circumstance grouping counts 18 self-inflicted deaths (Table 1, p. 712), while the coroners' or procurators fiscal's verdicts include 11 suicides and 8 open verdicts (p. 711); the paper does not reconcile its grouping with the legal verdicts, which matters for the Discussion's 29% self-harm figure.
